title: Loss Functions
hook: A loss function turns 'how wrong was I?' into a single number the model chases downhill — and the loss you pick decides what it learns to care about.
key_points: A loss maps the gap between prediction and target to one scalar to minimize.
Mean squared error suits regression; cross-entropy suits classification.
The choice of loss encodes your goal — what counts as a costly mistake.
Training is just gradient descent driving this number toward zero.
content_html: A loss function (or cost function) measures how far a model's predictions are from the truth, collapsing all the errors across your data into a single number. Training a model means adjusting its parameters to make that number as small as possible. The loss is the target everything else aims at — gradients, optimizers, and learning rates all exist to push it lower.
extra_html:
How it works

For regression you typically use mean squared error, which squares each prediction's distance from the target so large misses are penalized hard. For classification you use cross-entropy, which rewards the model for putting high probability on the correct class and punishes confident wrong answers severely. Whatever the form, the loss must be differentiable so backpropagation can compute how each parameter affects it.

Why it matters

The loss is where you smuggle your intentions into the math. Pick squared error and the model obsesses over outliers; pick something robust and it shrugs them off; add a penalty term and you discourage complexity. Choosing the right loss is often more consequential than choosing the model — it literally defines what "good" means for the rest of training.

related.hook: The 1986 paper that made deep learning possible: run the error backward through the network with the chain rule, and you get every weight's gradient in one sweep.

flashcards.prompt: What does a loss function do, in one sentence?
flashcards.back_html: It maps the gap between predictions and targets into a single scalar to minimize, collapsing all the errors across your data into one number.

flashcards.prompt: Which loss typically suits classification, and why?

choices.text: Cross-entropy — it rewards high probability on the correct class and punishes confident wrong answers
Mean squared error — it squares each prediction's distance from the target
Any loss works equally well for classification

flashcards.explanation_html: Cross-entropy suits classification; mean squared error suits regression, penalizing large misses by squaring the distance.

flashcards.prompt: Why must a loss function be differentiable?
flashcards.back_html: So backpropagation can compute how each parameter affects it — the gradients that drive training.
